## Objective Social Status (OSS)

Objective social status (OSS), or socioeconomic position, refers to the social and economic factors that shape the positions individuals hold in society's structure of inequality, and it has been conceptualised in two main ways [@wright_approaches_2005]. A gradational approach treats socioeconomic status (SES) as a continuum of resources, while a relational approach understands social class as a position in the labour market and in employment relations, captured through occupation-based schemes such as EGP [@erikson_casmin_1992] or, with greater attention to horizontal divisions in work logics, the scheme proposed by Oesch [-@oesch_redrawing_2006]. Each approach privileges different indicators. SES is usually measured through household income, which captures current command over resources, and educational attainment, which is more stable over the life course and also reflects cultural resources. Class relies on occupational information combined with employment status, and occupation-based measures are widely used because they offer reliable and parsimonious indicators of social position [@connelly_review_2016]. These indicators are correlated but not interchangeable, and each may relate to distributive attitudes through a different mechanism.

From a gradational perspective, the link between status and distributive preferences has been framed mainly in terms of self-interest: those with more resources benefit less from redistribution and support it less [@meltzer_rational_1981; @alesina_preferences_2011]. Income fits this logic most directly. Education is more ambiguous: it increases economic security, but it also shapes values and beliefs, so its association with redistributive preferences cannot be reduced to material interest [@gelepithis_inclusion_2022]. From a relational perspective, class differences in social attitudes have proved persistent, although their size and shape depend on national institutions [@svallfors_moral_2006; @lindh_class_2020]. Here, the mechanism lies less in current resources than in the risks and experiences attached to labour market positions. Workers whose skills or occupations expose them to income loss have stronger incentives to support social protection [@iversen_asset_2001; @rehm_risks_2009], and occupations operate as sites of preference formation through everyday work experiences [@kitschelt_occupations_2014].

Applied to market justice, both perspectives point in the same direction, but for different reasons. In gradational terms, those able to pay are the ones who gain from market-based access to social services, and the availability of private alternatives sharpens this divide, since it erodes support for public provision particularly among the middle and upper income classes [@busemeyer_welfare_2020]. In relational terms, those in more secure and advantaged positions depend less on the collective pooling of risks that public provision offers. Chile adds a particular configuration to this picture. Its inequality is concentrated at the very top of the income distribution, with considerably smaller differences across the rest of the class structure [@torche_unequal_2005]. If market justice preferences follow the ability to pay, the main divide should therefore separate the top of the distribution from everyone else, rather than run evenly along the status hierarchy. Existing evidence for Chile is consistent with a weak class gradient: in the case of pensions, differences between social classes in market justice preferences are positive but not statistically significant [@castillo_justification_2026].

Two limitations run through this literature. First, SES and class are rarely examined together, even though they may relate to market justice through different mechanisms: ability to pay in one case, position and risks in the labour market in the other. Second, most of the evidence is cross-sectional. Panel studies suggest that distributive preferences are fairly stable, anchored in long-term economic position and early socialisation, and shift mainly after large and often transitory changes in circumstances [@margalit_explaining_2013; @ogrady_how_2019]. Whether changes in an individual's objective position over time are associated with changes in market justice preferences, beyond stable differences between individuals, therefore remains an open question.
